text: Strangers who spent 45 minutes asking each other gradually deeper questions felt closer afterwards than pairs who stuck to small talk.
title: The Experimental Generation of Interpersonal Closeness: A Procedure and Some Preliminary Findings
evidence: Study 1 found greater postinteraction closeness with these tasks versus comparable small-talk tasks.

text: Couples who try just 7 minutes of something new and exciting together get a bigger lift in relationship quality than after a routine task.
title: Couples' shared participation in novel and arousing activities and experienced relationship quality
evidence: greater increases in experienced relationship quality from before to after participating together in a 7-min novel and arousing (vs. a more mundane) task

text: Couples whose partner usually greets their good news with real enthusiasm report more intimacy and higher day-to-day satisfaction.
title: What do you do when things go right? The intrapersonal and interpersonal benefits of sharing positive events
evidence: close relationships in which one's partner typically responds to capitalization attempts enthusiastically were associated with higher relationship well-being (e.g., intimacy, daily marital satisfaction)

text: How partners react to each other's good news predicts break-ups two months later more closely than how they react to bad news.
title: Will you be there for me when things go right? Supportive responses to positive event disclosures
evidence: 2 months later, responses to positive event discussions were more closely related to relationship well-being and break-up than were responses to negative event discussions

text: Partners who feel more appreciative of each other are more committed and more likely to still be together over time.
title: To have and to hold: gratitude promotes relationship maintenance in intimate bonds
evidence: are more committed and more likely to remain in their relationships over time

text: In one study, thank-yous that praised the partner, not just the favour, were linked to partners feeling more loved and understood.
title: Putting the "You" in "Thank You": Examining Other-Praising Behavior as the Active Relational Ingredient in Expressed Gratitude
evidence: Expresser's other-praising behavior was robustly positively associated with the benefactor's postinteraction perception of expresser responsiveness, personal good feelings in general, and felt loving in particular

text: Saying thanks out loud boosts your sense of how caring a relationship is more than just thinking grateful thoughts does.
title: Benefits of expressing gratitude: expressing gratitude to a partner changes one's view of the relationship
evidence: perceived communal strength was higher among participants in the expression-of-gratitude condition than among those in all three control conditions

text: Newlyweds still married six years later had turned toward each other's bids 86% of the time. Couples who divorced did so only 33% of the time.
title: Turn Towards Instead of Away
evidence: At the six-year follow-up, couples that stayed married turned towards one another 86% of the time. Couples that divorced averaged only 33% of the time.

text: In Gottman's studies of married couples, stable, happy pairs had about five positive moments for every negative one during conflict.
title: The Magic Relationship Ratio, According to Science
evidence: for every negative interaction during conflict, a stable and happy marriage has five (or more) positive interactions

text: Gottman's research suggests about two-thirds of couples' problems are perpetual: ongoing differences, not issues you solve once and for all.
title: P is for Problems
evidence: John Gottman’s research revealed that about ⅔ of relationship problems are unsolvable

text: In a study of 124 newlywed couples, the first three minutes of a disagreement predicted which marriages lasted over six years.
title: Predicting divorce among newlyweds from the first three minutes of a marital conflict discussion
evidence: It was possible to predict marital outcome over a 6-year period using just the first 3 minutes of data for both husbands and wives.

text: Gottman suggests couples who know each other's inner worlds in detail are better prepared to handle stress and conflict.
title: The Sound Relationship House: Build Love Maps
evidence: Couples who have detailed love maps of each other’s worlds are far better prepared to cope with stressful events and conflict.

text: The way newlyweds tell the story of their relationship predicted with 87.4% accuracy which couples later stayed married or split up.
title: Predicting marital stability and divorce in newlywed couples
evidence: predicted, with 87.4% accuracy, those couples whose marriages remained intact or broke up

text: Couples who spend more of a conversation laughing together rate their relationship as closer and more supportive.
title: Putting Laughter in Context: Shared Laughter as Behavioral Indicator of Relationship Well-Being
evidence: proportion of the conversation spent laughing simultaneously with the romantic partner was uniquely positively associated with global evaluations of relationship quality, closeness, and social support

text: In a small brain-scan study of wives, holding their husband's hand calmed the response to threat, more so in happier marriages.
title: Lending a hand: social regulation of the neural response to threat
evidence: higher marital quality predicting less threat-related neural activation in the right anterior insula, superior frontal gyrus, and hypothalamus during spousal, but not stranger, hand-holding

text: Couples who tackle stress as a team are more satisfied. A review of 72 samples found a strong link.
title: Dyadic coping and relationship satisfaction: A meta-analysis
evidence: The aggregated standardized zero-order correlation (r) for total dyadic coping with relationship satisfaction was .45

text: In a daily diary study, partner support, noticed or not, went with less sadness and a better relationship only when it met real needs.
title: The paradox of received social support: the importance of responsiveness
evidence: both visible and invisible support were beneficial (i.e., associated with less sadness and anxiety and with greater relationship quality) only when the support was responsive

text: Feeling understood, cared for and appreciated by a partner predicts healthier daily stress-hormone patterns 10 years later.
title: Perceived Partner Responsiveness Predicts Diurnal Cortisol Profiles 10 Years Later
evidence: Partner responsiveness predicted higher cortisol values at awakening and steeper (i.e., healthier) cortisol slopes at the 10-year follow-up

text: Couples who back each other's hopes for who they want to become tend to function better and stay together more.
title: Close partner as sculptor of the ideal self: behavioral affirmation and the Michelangelo phenomenon
evidence: perceived partner affirmation--particularly perceived partner behavioral affirmation--was strongly associated with quality of couple functioning and stability in ongoing relationships

text: People whose partner is happy to be leaned on when needed tend to be more independent and better at chasing their own goals.
title: The dependency paradox in close relationships: accepting dependence promotes independence
evidence: Results provided converging evidence in support of the proposed hypothesis.

text: Engaged and newlywed couples who did even a one-session relationship-awareness programme split up less over 3 years: 11% vs 24%.
title: Is skills training necessary for the primary prevention of marital distress and dissolution? A 3-year experimental study of three interventions
evidence: dissolved their relationships at a higher rate (24%) than couples completing PREP, CARE, and RA, who did not differ on rates of dissolution (11%)

text: Couples who talk openly about sex tend to be more satisfied, both in their sex life and in the relationship overall.
title: Dimensions of couples' sexual communication, relationship satisfaction, and sexual satisfaction: A meta-analysis
evidence: evidenced a positive association between sexual communication and both relationship (r = .37) and sexual satisfaction (r = .43)

text: How well couples talk about intimacy is more closely linked to satisfaction than how often they talk about it.
title: Dimensions of couples' sexual communication, relationship satisfaction, and sexual satisfaction: A meta-analysis
evidence: the effect size for quality of sexual communication (r = .43; .52) was larger compared to the frequency of sexual communication (r = .31; .31)

text: In couples becoming parents, partners who were understanding when the other wasn't in the mood reported more sexual and relationship satisfaction.
title: Understanding When a Partner Is Not in the Mood: Sexual Communal Strength in Couples Transitioning to Parenthood
evidence: the motivation to be understanding about a partner's need not to engage in sex is uniquely associated with sexual and relationship satisfaction

text: People tend to underestimate how much a new conversation partner likes them and enjoyed talking with them. This is called the liking gap.
title: The Liking Gap in Conversations: Do People Like Us More Than We Think?
evidence: people systematically underestimated how much their conversation partners liked them and enjoyed their company, an illusion we call the liking gap

text: The liking gap isn't only a first-meeting thing. Among new student dorm mates, it lasted for several months.
title: The Liking Gap in Conversations: Do People Like Us More Than We Think?
evidence: The liking gap persisted in conversations of varying lengths and even lasted for several months, as college dorm mates developed new relationships.

text: Commuters asked to chat with a stranger had a nicer journey than those told to keep to themselves, and felt no less productive.
title: Mistakenly seeking solitude
evidence: participants reported a more positive (and no less productive) experience when they connected than when they did not

text: Commuters dread starting a chat more than the chat itself, mainly because they wrongly expect the other person won't be interested.
title: Hello, stranger? Pleasant conversations are preceded by concerns about starting one
evidence: Commuters predicted that trying to have a conversation would be less pleasant than actually having one because they anticipated that others would be uninterested

text: People expect to learn less from talking with someone than they actually learn.
title: Talking with strangers is surprisingly informative
evidence: Participants who were asked to talk with another person expected to learn significantly less from the conversation than they actually reported learning afterward

text: Conversations with strangers feel less awkward than people predict, and they leave people happier and more connected than expected.
title: Overly shallow?: Miscalibrated expectations create a barrier to deeper conversation
evidence: conversations between strangers felt less awkward, and created more connectedness and happiness, than the participants themselves expected

text: After having both kinds of chat, people feel more connected to a partner they talked deeply with than to one they made small talk with.
title: Overly shallow?: Miscalibrated expectations create a barrier to deeper conversation
evidence: they also felt more connected to deep conversation partners than shallow conversation partners after having both types of conversations

text: Strangers care more about what you share than you expect. People underestimate how interested others are in their disclosures.
title: Overly shallow?: Miscalibrated expectations create a barrier to deeper conversation
evidence: participants expected others to care less about their disclosures in conversation than others actually did

text: People who ask more questions, especially follow-up questions, are liked more by the person they're talking with.
title: It doesn't hurt to ask: Question-asking increases liking
evidence: people who ask more questions, particularly follow-up questions, are better liked by their conversation partners

text: Speed daters who ask more follow-up questions are more likely to get a yes for a second date.
title: It doesn't hurt to ask: Question-asking increases liking
evidence: speed daters who ask more follow-up questions during their dates are more likely to elicit agreement for second dates from their partners

text: People spend 30 to 40% of their speech telling others about their own experiences.
title: Disclosing information about the self is intrinsically rewarding
evidence: Humans devote 30-40% of speech output solely to informing others of their own subjective experiences.

text: Talking about yourself is linked to more activity in the brain's reward areas, and people will even give up money to do it.
title: Disclosing information about the self is intrinsically rewarding
evidence: Self-disclosure was strongly associated with increased activation in brain regions that form the mesolimbic dopamine system

text: People who share more personal things tend to be liked more than people who keep it surface-level.
title: Self-disclosure and liking: a meta-analytic review
evidence: People who engage in intimate disclosures tend to be liked more than people who disclose at lower levels

text: Pairs who spend 45 minutes on gradually deeper sharing tasks feel closer afterwards than pairs given small-talk tasks.
title: The Experimental Generation of Interpersonal Closeness: A Procedure and Some Preliminary Findings
evidence: Study 1 found greater postinteraction closeness with these tasks versus comparable small-talk tasks.

text: In one study, 46% of the happiest people's conversations were substantive, against 22% for the least happy.
title: Eavesdropping on Happiness: Well-being is Related to Having Less Small Talk and More Substantive Conversations
evidence: They also had roughly one third as much small talk (10.2% vs. 28.3%) and twice as many substantive conversations (45.9% vs. 21.8%

text: People who spent more hours with a new acquaintance, especially doing fun things, tended to become closer friends.
title: How many hours does it take to make a friend?
evidence: Hours together was associated with closer friendships. Time spent engaging in leisure activities also predicted closeness.

text: People writing thank-you letters underestimate how good the recipient will feel and overestimate how awkward it will be.
title: Undervaluing Gratitude: Expressers Misunderstand the Consequences of Showing Appreciation
evidence: overestimated how awkward recipients would feel, and underestimated how positive recipients would feel

text: People giving a compliment underestimate how good it will make the other person feel.
title: Why a Simple Act of Kindness Is Not as Simple as It Seems: Underestimating the Positive Impact of Our Compliments on Others
evidence: compliment givers underestimated how positively the person receiving their compliment would feel

text: Lonely people who felt more nostalgic also tended to feel they had more people to lean on.
title: Counteracting loneliness: on the restorative function of nostalgia
evidence: Nostalgia, in turn, increased perceptions of social support.

text: Writing about a value that really matters to you brings out feelings of love and connection toward others.
title: Why does writing about important values reduce defensiveness? Self-affirmation and the role of positive other-directed feelings
evidence: participants who wrote about an important value reported more positive other-directed feelings, such as love and connection

text: Curious people can feel close to a new person even during small talk, not just in deep conversations.
title: When curiosity breeds intimacy: taking advantage of intimacy opportunities and transforming boring conversations
evidence: curious people felt close to partners during intimate and small-talk conversations

text: Students feel happier and more like they belong on days when they talk with more classmates than usual.
title: Social Interactions and Well-Being: The Surprising Power of Weak Ties
evidence: students experienced greater happiness and greater feelings of belonging on days when they interacted with more classmates than usual

text: After laughing at a funny video, people's self-disclosures were rated as more intimate by others, though they didn't notice it themselves.
title: Laughter's influence on the intimacy of self-disclosure
evidence: disclosure intimacy is significantly higher after laughter than in the control condition

text: Google interviewed more than 200 of its own teams and found that feeling safe to take risks in front of each other mattered most.
title: Five dynamics of an effective team (Think with Google)
evidence: Psychological safety: This was the most important dynamic in an effective team.

text: At Google, how teammates get on and work together counts for far more than who is actually on the team.
title: Five dynamics of an effective team (Think with Google)
evidence: At Google, who is on a team matters much less than how team members interact, structure their work, and view their contributions.

text: In 51 factory teams, those who felt safe to speak up did more learning together, and teams that learned more tended to perform better.
title: Psychological Safety and Learning Behavior in Work Teams
evidence: As predicted, learning behavior mediates between team psychological safety and team performance.

text: Singing together bonds strangers fast. New singing classes felt close sooner than craft or writing classes, which only caught up later.
title: The ice-breaker effect: singing mediates fast social bonding
evidence: This represents the first evidence for an 'ice-breaker effect' of singing in promoting fast cohesion between unfamiliar individuals

text: In small studies, people who'd laughed together could take a bit more pain afterwards, seemingly from the laughing itself, not just a good mood.
title: Social laughter is correlated with an elevated pain threshold
evidence: This pain-tolerance effect is due to laughter itself and not simply due to a change in positive affect.

text: In experiments, people who'd moved in time together cooperated more afterwards, even when it cost them something.
title: Synchrony and cooperation
evidence: Across three experiments, people acting in synchrony with others cooperated more in subsequent group economic exercises, even in situations requiring personal sacrifice.

text: Dancing in time with others and dancing with energy each help a group bond, and each raises how much pain dancers can take.
title: Synchrony and exertion during dance independently raise pain threshold and encourage social bonding
evidence: Both demonstrated significant independent positive effects on pain threshold (a proxy for endorphin activation) and in-group bonding.

text: In a silent disco study, strangers who danced in time with each other felt more bonded and could take more pain.
title: Silent disco: dancing in synchrony leads to elevated pain thresholds and social closeness
evidence: Similarly, those in the synchrony condition reported being more socially bonded

text: People tend to underestimate how likely others are to say yes when asked directly for help, in some studies by as much as half.
title: If you need help, just ask: underestimating compliance with direct requests for help
evidence: people underestimated by as much as 50% the likelihood that others would agree to a direct request for help

text: Owning up to a mistake or asking for help feels risky to you, but others tend to see it in a kinder light than you expect.
title: Beautiful mess effect: Self-other differences in evaluation of showing vulnerability
evidence: focus more on the positive aspects of showing vulnerability, and, therefore, evaluate it more positively

text: A thank-you makes people feel valued, so they help more. Fundraisers made more calls after their manager thanked them.
title: A little thanks goes a long way: Explaining why gratitude expressions motivate prosocial behavior
evidence: A manager's gratitude expression increased the number of calls made by university fundraisers

text: In US college sororities, new members who felt more grateful during gift week had closer relationships with each other a month later.
title: Beyond reciprocity: gratitude and relationships in everyday life
evidence: gratitude during the week predicted future relationship outcomes. Gratitude may function to promote relationship formation and maintenance.

text: People hold back sincere compliments partly because they underestimate how much those compliments will brighten someone's day.
title: Insufficiently complimentary?: Underestimating the positive impact of compliments creates a barrier to expressing them
evidence: a reluctance to express genuine compliments partly stems from underestimating the positive impact that compliments will have on recipients

text: People who look embarrassed are seen as kinder and more generous, and others trust them more.
title: Flustered and faithful: embarrassment as a signal of prosociality
evidence: In turn, observers respond with affiliative behaviors toward the signaler, including greater trust and desire to affiliate with the embarrassed individual.

text: Going through something uncomfortable together helps strangers bond and cooperate more. Shared hardship can glue a group together.
title: Pain as social glue: shared pain increases cooperation
evidence: Sharing painful experiences with other people, compared with a no-pain control treatment, promoted trusting interpersonal relationships by increasing perceived bonding among strangers

text: After 20 minutes of improv games, people felt more upbeat and more at ease with uncertainty than after other group activities.
title: Improv experience promotes divergent thinking, uncertainty tolerance, and affective well-being
evidence: provides new findings that improv can boost positive affect and increase uncertainty tolerance relative to other social interactions
